instrument_classification.asset_class: forex (demonstrated: GBP AUD, NZDUSD); also taught as applicable to metals, indices, and reported cryptocurrency use
instrument_classification.instrument: GBP AUD and NZDUSD (the two worked examples)
instrument_classification.rationale: The educator states the strategy applies to basically all assets, names forex/metals/indices, and reports crypto use secondhand rather than personally.
instrument_classification.transcript_quote: as I said at the beginning of the video this strategy is applicable to basically all assets. So of course the forex market like I've been showing you here today. It's also great for metals and indices and I also know a lot of people who use it in the cryptocurrency market. I don't personally but I've heard that there's been a lot of success with that.

strategies.name: Four-item checklist 15-minute strategy: 4H premium/discount alignment + liquidity sweep + break of structure with imbalance + 71% Fibonacci retracement limit entry
strategies.direction_transcript_quote: anything above 50% of the trading range is considered premium and we should only be looking for selling opportunities. Now, anything below the 50% is considered discount pricing and we would only want to be looking for buying opportunities.
strategies.higher_timeframe_transcript_quote: And the 4our time frame is going to act as our higher time frame to form a bias and anchor that bias to at all times.
strategies.execution_timeframe_transcript_quote: The 15-minut time frame is going to be our execution time frame where we actually place trades.

setup.description: The strategy is a four-item checklist: higher-timeframe alignment, liquidity sweep, break of structure plus imbalance, and a 71% retracement.
setup.transcript_quote: We have higher time frame alignment, liquidity sweep, break of structure plus imbalance, and a 71% retracement.

setup.description: The 15-minute trade bias should align with the higher-timeframe bias so the trade is on the side of the overarching trend, which prevents unnecessary losses.
setup.transcript_quote: If we can align our 15minute trade bias to a higher time frame bias, which is the overarching trend, then more times than not, we'll be on the right side of the market, and it'll prevent a lot of unnecessary losses.

setup.description: The premise of higher-timeframe alignment is gauging premium and discount pricing within a trading range.
setup.transcript_quote: So, the premise of higher time frame alignment is premium and discount. Whenever we have a trading range, we want to gauge premium and discount pricing.

setup.description: The educator's indicator automatically computes premium/discount specifically on the 4-hour timeframe.
setup.transcript_quote: So, my indicator automatically checks premium and discount on the higher time frame. As you can see here, I have it set to 4hour.

setup.description: Core premise of the whole strategy: buy low, sell high.
setup.transcript_quote: The strategy is very simplistic. We buy low and sell high.

setup.description: Liquidity is resting money in the market, most commonly found at major highs and major lows, which the market purges to fuel the next move.
setup.transcript_quote: The simple way to describe liquidity is just resting money in the market. And the market wants to purge that liquidity and bring that money back in to add fuel for the next move. The most common area to find resting liquidity is major highs and major lows.

setup.description: The custom indicator automates chart annotation, but the same steps can be done manually without it.
setup.transcript_quote: It's a great tool to have, but you don't need it. You can do all of the things I'm about to teach you today manually on your own.

setup.description: A free equivalent for the structure/fractal annotations exists on TradingView (fractals or Williams fractals).
setup.transcript_quote: There's a free version of these little arrows if you search on Trading View fractals or Williams fractals. It's completely free.

setup.description: An imbalance/fair value gap is a three-candlestick pattern with a gap between the first candle's low and the third candle's high, formed by a straight move with no buy/sell equilibrium.
setup.transcript_quote: it's a three candlestick pattern. 1 2 3. And between the low of this first candle and the high of the third candle, we can see that there is a very large gap. That was a period of time where there was only a straight move to the downside. There was no equilibrium between buying and selling, which is why it's called imbalance.

setup.description: Price is typically drawn back to fill an imbalance/fair value gap before continuing in its original direction.
setup.transcript_quote: Now, whenever this occurs on the chart, price is drawn back towards it. So, after we move away from it significantly, typically price will retrace until it fills that gap and then it will often continue in its intended direction.

setup.description: The Fibonacci retracement tool is used only as a measurement/framing tool, not as an indicator or a reaction level.
setup.transcript_quote: The Fibonacci retracement tool is not an indicator. It is not a strategy in and of itself. The way I use it is simply as a measurement tool. It helps me frame my trade. So don't be under the impression that somehow these retracement levels are magic numbers that price will react to. That is absolutely not the case.

setup.description: Fibonacci tool settings: deselect all levels, enable only 71% and 75% (plus 0 and 1); only the 71% is actually used for entry.
setup.transcript_quote: You just deselect everything and enable the levels you want. So I have the 71% and the 75%. Really only use the 71%. But yeah, just deselect everything that you don't want. Only enable the ones that you do want, of course, including the zero and the one.

setup.description: The Fibonacci range is drawn from the low to the high of the leg (stated explicitly in the second, long-side example).
setup.transcript_quote: So, all I do is break out the Fibonacci tool, start at the low, click, and drag to the high.

setup.description: The magnet tool should be set to weak magnet rather than strong magnet, which snaps entry/stop/target more accurately to candle wicks.
setup.transcript_quote: To make this easier, you can use the magnet tool on Trading View. Just set it to weak magnet instead of strong magnet. I find that you fight it a lot less when it's just the weak magnet.

entry_sequence.action: Determine directional bias from the 4-hour timeframe: above 50% of the trading range is premium (look only for sells); below 50% is discount (look only for buys).
entry_sequence.rationale: Checklist item 1 -- higher timeframe alignment sets which direction is even eligible on the 15-minute chart.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: anything above 50% of the trading range is considered premium and we should only be looking for selling opportunities. Now, anything below the 50% is considered discount pricing and we would only want to be looking for buying opportunities.

entry_sequence.action: Identify a liquidity sweep: a wick piercing beyond a recent major high or low, purging resting liquidity and adding fuel for the next move.
entry_sequence.rationale: Checklist item 2 -- confirms institutional participation and which side has just had liquidity purged.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: if we look all the way to the right, this large wick right here pierced above that previous high, purging all of that liquidity, bringing that money back into the market, adding fuel for the next upcoming move. So this is what's referred to as buyside liquidity because the liquidity was purged to the upside.

entry_sequence.action: After a sweep on one side, treat the untested relative-equal highs/lows on the opposite side as price's likely next objective.
entry_sequence.rationale: Establishes where price is expected to travel next, which is the same side the eventual target sits on.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: Now this tells us that there's a high likelihood of selling opportunities being favored now because the liquidity was already purged to the upside. So now the next objective of price would be to purge liquidity from the downside. And where can we identify that next objective? Well, the most recent major lows right here. So, those are pretty untested relative equal lows. And it's safe to say that the objective of price would be most likely to head in that direction to purge liquidity from those lows.

entry_sequence.action: Wait for a break of structure -- a structural major high or low violated, printing a BOS label.
entry_sequence.rationale: Checklist item 3a -- the break of structure signals a potential trading opportunity exists.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: So whenever one of these structural lows or highs vice versa is violated, you'll see this BOS label printed, which of course stands for break of structure. That signals to me that there has been a significant movement in price and that there is a potential trading opportunity on the horizon.

entry_sequence.action: Do not enter at the break of structure itself; wait for a retracement, which typically runs toward the fair value gap/imbalance.
entry_sequence.rationale: Checklist item 3b -- entering immediately at BOS would violate the buy-low/sell-high premise.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: So we don't just immediately enter when there's a break of structure because that would be selling low and we don't want to do that obviously. So when a break of structure occurs, we need to patiently wait for a retracement. Now, typically that retracement ends up being towards a fair value gap or an imbalance.

entry_sequence.action: Place the entry at the 71% Fibonacci retracement level (short-side example).
entry_sequence.rationale: Checklist item 4 -- the 71% is the stated entry level once the Fibonacci range is drawn over the retracement leg.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: I place my entry at the 71% right here.

entry_sequence.action: The order must be a pending limit order, not a market execution, since the trade is set up in advance of price reaching the level.
entry_sequence.rationale: The setup is built ahead of price arriving at the 71% level.
entry_sequence.transcript_quote: Now, because we're setting up a trade in advance, you would have to do a pending limit order, which means you're betting that price will get to this point at some point in time. So, that obviously differs from a market execution where you're entering right away in real time. So, it's really important to note you have to use pending limit orders for this strategy.

confluences.name: Fibonacci 71% aligned with the imbalance/fair value gap (A+ setup)
confluences.description: When the 71% entry level coincides with the fair value gap, the trade is treated as higher probability with expected minimal drawdown.
confluences.transcript_quote: And that is when the Fibonacci retracement number lines up with the imbalance or fair value gap. Remember what I said about imbalances and fair value gaps. It's a reaction point for price. Price wants to fill that gap and then continue it in its intended direction. So if we can line up our entry with that fair value gap, odds are we're not going to have significant draw down.

confluences.name: A+ setup definition
confluences.description: The full four-item checklist plus the Fibonacci/fair-value-gap alignment together define an A+ setup with a very high likelihood of success.
confluences.transcript_quote: Make your Fibonacci numbers line up with the fair value gap or imbalance. So, if you can do that combined with the other things that I've listed here, that is what I like to call an A+ setup and you have a very high likelihood of success.

confluences.name: Wick rejection (liquidity grab) distinguished from a body-close break of structure
confluences.description: A sweep made by a wick rather than a candle body close is a liquidity grab signalling insufficient momentum to continue, and therefore rejection back the other way.
confluences.transcript_quote: The reason this is a liquidity grab instead of a break of structure is because it was a wick instead of candle body closure. If you compare the candle body closure here to the candlestick here, there's a big difference. And I hope you guys can see that. Whenever a wick is forming like that, that means there was not enough momentum to actually break through and continue. But instead, it rejected from that area and continue to push up from there.

confluences.name: Opposite-side liquidity remaining unpurged confirms the setup
confluences.description: Relative-equal levels on the opposite side (rather than a fresh purge of them) confirm price is likely to push through and take that liquidity; a fresh purge on that side would instead read as indecision, not a trade setup.
confluences.transcript_quote: If this candlestick right here went higher and purged liquidity from this high, that would be a different story. This would probably just be indecision and I would not even consider it as a trade setup. But because we made these relative equal highs, that tells me price is highly likely to push higher once more, taking out all of this liquidity.

stop.anchor: High of the Fibonacci retracement range (short-side, GBP AUD example).
stop.rationale: The stop is dragged to the extreme of the Fibonacci range used to frame the trade, snapped to the wick using the weak-magnet tool.
stop.transcript_quote: I simply drag the stop-loss to the high of the Fibonacci range right here.

targets.type: Low of the Fibonacci retracement range (short-side, GBP AUD example); entering at 71% yields a stated risk-to-reward of 2.45.
targets.rationale: Take-profit is dragged to the low of the same Fibonacci range that defines the stop.
targets.transcript_quote: If I target the 71% from my entry, I get a risk-to-reward ratio of 2.45. That of course means for every dollar that I'm risking, I would gain two and a half roughly in return if it's a successful trade. So once again, I use the retracement tool as a way to frame my trade. So using the short position tool on Trading View, I place my entry at the 71% right here. I simply drag the stop-loss to the high of the Fibonacci range right here. And then I drag the takerit to the low of the Fibonacci range right here.

management.rule: The trade idea remains valid until either endpoint of the Fibonacci range is violated; a sharp reaction that fails to violate the range low is not a reason to cancel the pending order.
management.transcript_quote: You can see that this low here did not violate the low of the Fibonacci range. That's a very important detail because if our trade was based on this high and this low, then technically the trade still remains valid until one of those levels are violated. If neither of those levels have been violated, then the trade idea is still intact and there's logically no reason to delete the order.

management.rule: Minor overshoot past the 71% entry (pushing a little past the 75%) is treated as minimal drawdown, not invalidation.
management.transcript_quote: You can see that it pushed past the 71, a little bit past the 75, but overall that is very minimal draw down in the grand scheme of things.

management.rule: Drawdown is defined as price spending time close to the stop-loss before reacting toward the target.
management.transcript_quote: Anytime that price is spending in this dark gray area close to my stop loss, that's considered draw down. That's when you're going to see those big red numbers adding up and growing, and we obviously don't want that.

management.rule: Even with the full confluence stack present, drawdown and losing trades still occur; nothing is guaranteed.
management.transcript_quote: Ideally, of course, the markets are imperfect. It doesn't always work like this. Even if all the confluences line up, we sometimes still get draw down and losing trades. Of course, nothing is 100% in the market. But what we can do is try our best to mitigate it.

variants.name: Long-side mirror (NZDUSD example)
variants.rule: Entry at 71% long; stop snapped to the wick at the low of the Fibonacci range; target at the high of the Fibonacci range.
variants.transcript_quote: Now using the magnet tool again, I can click the stop loss, drag it over to that wick, and it'll snap right to it. Same thing goes for my takerit. Click this little button at the top, drag it to the high of the Fibonacci range, and drop it.

variants.name: Internal/imperfect break of structure accepted
variants.rule: An internal break of structure -- not only a clean major-structure break -- still satisfies the break-of-structure checklist item.
variants.transcript_quote: The break of structure is not very clear here. This is more so an internal breakup structure, but it is a breaker structure nonetheless.

source_gaps.reason: The transcript says premium/discount is measured against 'a trading range' on the 4-hour and that the indicator computes it automatically, but never states which swing high and swing low define that range, how far back it looks, or how it is redrawn.

Only the long example explicitly states the draw direction ('start at the low, click, and drag to the high'). The transcript never defines which low and which high -- whether they are the sweep extreme, the break-of-structure leg, the fractal swing points, or the imbalance boundaries -- so the exact anchors are unresolved for both examples.
Structure points come from the educator's indicator or from 'fractals or Williams fractals', but no period/length setting or definition of 'major' versus minor swing is given.
No stated minimum penetration depth, wick size, or number of candles that makes a wick beyond a prior high/low count as a sweep, nor how recent the swept level must be.

The checklist implies an order (alignment, sweep, break of structure + imbalance, 71% retracement) but the transcript never states a maximum number of bars or time between the sweep, the break of structure, and the retracement, nor whether the break of structure must occur after the sweep in all cases.
Multiple fair value gaps can exist inside a leg; the transcript does not say which imbalance to use when more than one is present, nor any minimum gap size.
The A+ confluence requires the 71% level to 'line up' with the fair value gap, but no tolerance is defined (touching the gap, inside the gap, within N pips).

The 75% level is enabled in the Fibonacci settings and referenced when describing drawdown ('pushed past the 71, a little bit past the 75'), but the transcript explicitly says only the 71% is used and never assigns the 75% an executable role.
The only stated invalidation is violation of one of the Fibonacci range endpoints; no time-based expiry, bar-count limit, or rule for cancelling an unfilled order is given.
The transcript gives a risk-to-reward figure (2.45) but never states risk per trade, lot sizing, account risk percentage, or maximum concurrent positions.
No trading session, time-of-day window, news filter, or day-of-week restriction is taught anywhere in the transcript.
Once filled, the transcript shows only a fixed stop and fixed take-profit; no partial take-profit, breakeven move, or trailing rule is taught.
The transcript does not address what to do if the stop is hit and the same higher-timeframe bias persists, or whether a second setup may be taken in the same leg.

top_level_source_gaps.reason: The transcript teaches exactly one strategy. The GBP AUD and NZDUSD sections are two worked examples of the same four-item checklist (the second explicitly framed as the 'not so pretty' example), not two separate strategies.

The educator's custom indicator computes premium/discount, prints BOS labels, marks fractal highs/lows, and draws fair value gaps. Its internal logic and settings are not disclosed, so any automated reproduction of those annotations is not settled by the source.
No win rate, expectancy, sample size, or backtest results are provided; the only quantitative claim is the 2.45 risk-to-reward geometry of the 71% entry.
The strategy is claimed to work on forex, metals, indices and crypto, but no per-asset parameter differences, spread/commission handling, or instrument-specific adjustments are taught.
